prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

By menopause, it’s not just estrogen my mother lacks. She’s lost her eldest son— that’s me, the one who’s queer—the doctor who once made her very proud. These days, I do my own wash when I’m home, I cook for her so she can take a break from all the chores she now refuses to assign to me. She sits, half-watching Ricki through her tea’s thin steam, her squint of disapproval more denial than it is disgust. She hears much better than she sees—it’s easier to keep out vision than it is to clear the air of sounds—and yet I know it’s age that stultifies her senses too. Enraged because she’s lost so much, I understand why suddenly she looks so stunned as from the television: “. . . Bitch, she stole my boyfriend, my own mother did! . . .” I fold a towel noiselessly. I know she thinks it’s garbage, sinful, crap—just as she thinks that taking estrogen in pills is not what God intended, no matter what the doctors say; or that I’m gay is plain unnatural, she can’t endure such pain. The oven timer rings. The cookies that I’ve baked are done. I’ll make another batch though she won’t touch them: given up for Lent. My mother’s love. I wonder where it went.

Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: She, These, Ricki

outputs.L1:
With menopause, it is not only estrogen that my mother lacks. She has lost her eldest son—that is, me, the queer one, the doctor who once made her so proud. These days, when I am home, I do my own laundry. I cook for her, giving her a respite from the chores she now refuses to assign me. She sits half-watching *Ricki* through the faint steam rising from her tea, her disapproving squint conveying more denial than disgust. She hears far better than she sees—it is easier to shut out what is visible than to clear the air of sound—though I know that age, too, has dulled her senses.

Enraged by all she has lost, I understand why she suddenly looks so stunned when the television erupts: “. . . Bitch, she stole my boyfriend, my own mother did! . . .” I fold a towel without a sound. I know she thinks it is garbage, sinful, mere crap—just as she believes that taking estrogen in pill form is not what God intended, regardless of what the doctors say, and that my being gay is simply unnatural, a pain she cannot endure.

The oven timer rings. The cookies I baked are ready. I will make another batch, though she will not touch them: she has given them up for Lent. My mother’s love—I wonder where it went.
outputs.L2:
Menopause has deprived my mother of more than estrogen. In her mind, she has also been bereaved of her firstborn son: me, the queer one, the physician who used to fill her with pride. Whenever I visit now, I launder my own clothes and prepare meals to relieve her of some work, because she no longer permits herself to ask me to help with household tasks. Through the faint vapor rising from her tea, she only partly attends to *Ricki*. Her narrowed, condemning gaze seems rooted less in revulsion than in refusal to accept what she sees. Her hearing remains sharper than her eyesight; images can be shut out more easily than voices can be removed from a room. Still, I recognize that age has dulled both senses.

Her anger comes from having endured so many losses, so I understand the shock on her face when the television erupts: “. . . Bitch, she stole my boyfriend, my own mother did! . . .” Without making a sound, I crease a towel. I know she regards the program as trash—vulgar, immoral nonsense. She feels the same way about swallowing estrogen tablets: regardless of medical advice, she believes God never meant for it to be done. And my being gay, to her, is simply against nature, an agony she cannot bear.

Then the kitchen timer sounds. The cookies I made are ready. I will bake another tray, even though she has renounced them for Lent and will eat none. I think about my mother’s love and ask myself where it has disappeared.
outputs.L3:
The speaker’s mother feels as though she has lost her eldest son since learning that he is queer. Once, she took pride in his accomplishments, especially his career as a doctor, but that pride has been overshadowed by her inability to accept his identity. Her religious beliefs shape this rejection: she considers both estrogen treatment and her son’s sexuality unnatural and incompatible with her understanding of faith.

Even so, the speaker continues to care for her. When he visits home, he does the laundry, cooks meals, and takes on small tasks to ease her burden, despite her efforts to distance him from household responsibilities. He understands that her anger and disapproval are not rooted solely in religion; they also arise from the pain of aging, loss, and a life marked by emotional hardship. This awareness allows him to respond with compassion, even when her words wound him.

Through gestures such as baking cookies and helping around the house, the speaker keeps expressing his love. Yet these acts of care are accompanied by grief. While his mother believes she has lost the son she once knew, he mourns a different loss: the apparent disappearance of the love she once gave him so freely.
outputs.L4:
My mother and I used to understand each other through small, ordinary acts. We folded laundry together, washed dishes after dinner, and sat in front of the television while the evening settled around us. Caring for the house was once a kind of shared language, a way of expressing affection without having to name it. But as she grew older and I became more honest about my queerness, those familiar routines changed. The same rooms remained, yet the intimacy that had filled them began to disappear.

Her faith shaped the distance between us. She could accept my help, but not the truth of who I was. Religion gave her a language of sin, denial, and correction, allowing her to treat my identity as a temporary mistake rather than part of her child. She avoided direct conversations, turned her attention toward chores or television, and behaved as though silence might erase what she did not want to acknowledge. Even when we sat beside each other, the screen offered an easier reality than the one we shared.

Her aging body deepened my awareness of what was being lost. Menopause marked a transition she could not prevent, a reminder that time was changing her even as she resisted change in me. I watched her become more vulnerable and tried to care for her through practical gestures. I cleaned, prepared food, and attended to the domestic tasks that had once united us. These acts were expressions of love, but they were also attempts to recover the mother I remembered—the woman whose care had once seemed unconditional.

Food became another measure of our estrangement. A meal could signify welcome, belonging, and maternal protection; withholding it could communicate rejection more sharply than words. When she no longer fed me with the same tenderness, the absence carried emotional weight. Hunger became more than a physical condition. It represented the affection, recognition, and security she refused to offer. What was missing from the table reflected what was missing from our relationship.

Still, I continued to care for her. My attention to her needs was not enough to restore our former closeness, because the rupture between us could not be repaired through labor alone. I could wash every dish, fold every piece of clothing, and bring her every comfort, but I could not make her see me without judgment. Love persisted between us, yet it had been distorted by prejudice and fear. Her faith, instead of enlarging her compassion, became a barrier behind which she concealed her rejection.

The deepest pain came from knowing that maternal love had not vanished entirely. It remained present in fragments—in old habits, shared memories, and moments of unspoken concern—but it no longer offered refuge. My mother’s love endured only in a damaged form, constrained by what she believed I should be. As she aged, I grieved not only the possibility of losing her to time, but also the bond we had already lost. My efforts to care for her could honor that bond, but they could not bring it back.
outputs.L5: She found Ricki waiting beneath the old oak tree, holding a bundle of letters tied with blue ribbon. “These belong to you,” Ricki said with a gentle smile. As she opened the first envelope, memories returned—of summer afternoons, shared secrets, and promises neither of them had forgotten.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem from the perspective of a gay doctor visiting his aging, devoutly religious mother, who struggles to accept his sexuality. Include domestic chores, menopause, television, Lent, and a final reflection on maternal love.
counterfactuals.output:
I come home with a stethoscope in my suitcase, though she has asked me not to examine her, only to change the furnace filter and reach the blue bowl above the refrigerator. Dust whitens my hands like ash. In the kitchen I wash cups, scrape wax from the tablecloth, carry laundry down the narrow stairs while she follows, naming every shirt I ruined as a boy. The house is smaller now, or perhaps I have become too large for the version of me she keeps here.

At supper she tells me menopause was a long country she crossed without a map: the sudden heat, the vanished blood, the nights she lay beside my father listening to her own heart gallop. I tell her the body is faithful even in its betrayals. She says, You always did know how to make suffering sound official.

Afterward we watch television with the volume high. A game show spills applause into the room; strangers win vacations, cars, bright kitchens. During the commercials she asks if I am still seeing him, as if love were a symptom that should have cleared by now. I say yes. She folds a dish towel into smaller and smaller squares. On the screen, everyone embraces beneath falling confetti.

It is Lent. She has given up sugar and, perhaps, questions she cannot bear to hear answered. Each morning she kneels before the little crucifix in the hallway. Each morning I count the seconds before she rises, ready to catch her if her knees fail. She prays for my soul. I check her blood pressure. We practice our separate faiths.

On Friday I vacuum the living room, salt the icy steps, sort her pills into their plastic compartments: morning, noon, evening, night. She stands at the sink peeling potatoes and says God made me. I wait. She does not say wrong. Steam gathers on the window, making the bare trees mercifully indistinct.

Before bed, she leaves a blanket outside my door, though I have told her I am not cold. I understand this is the language she has left: covered dishes, clean sheets, a hand hovering near my fevered forehead but not quite touching. Maternal love, I think, is not always acceptance. Sometimes it is a locked church with one candle burning; sometimes the key is lost, sometimes both of us stand outside in the weather. Still, through the stained glass, a little warmth reaches us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical first-person monologue about a queer eldest son whose mother treats him as though she has lost him after he comes out. Set the scene at home while he folds laundry and bakes cookies for her.
counterfactuals.output:
The dryer hums in the basement like something trying not to cry.

I fold her blouses first, smoothing the sleeves along their old creases, matching each cuff to its twin. Then towels, warm as bread. Then my youngest brother’s shirts, still carrying the faint green scent of grass despite the wash. I have always been good at making order from what comes out tangled.

Upstairs, the oven warms the kitchen. Butter softens in a blue bowl. I measure sugar with the same cup she used when I was small enough to stand on a chair beside her, eldest son, first miracle, little man of the house. She would guide my wrist as I stirred and laugh when flour rose around us like weather.

Now she moves through the rooms as if I am weather.

Since I told her, she looks at me with the solemn tenderness people reserve for photographs of the dead. I have not gone anywhere. I am here, pairing her socks, scraping the mixing bowl clean. Still, she speaks of me in the past tense when she prays.

My son was such a happy boy.

My son used to tell me everything.

As though honesty were the locked door between us. As though I had not opened it.

I cream the butter and sugar until they become one pale thing. Vanilla. Eggs. Flour sifted fine. The recipe is hers, written on an index card in a slanting hand: *Do not overmix.* I know better than to think love follows instructions. I overmix nothing. I ruin nothing. I press each mound of dough onto the baking sheet with careful fingers and leave room for spreading.

She sits at the kitchen table without looking at me. Her grief has made a shrine of her body: folded hands, lowered eyes, mouth arranged around a name she thinks she has lost.

I want to ask her whom she is mourning.

The child who carried grocery bags before his arms were strong enough? The boy who learned everyone’s birthdays, who stayed up with feverish siblings, who called when he was late? He is here. I am all my former selves at once, standing barefoot on cold tile, wearing an apron dusted white.

The cookies begin to sweeten the house. Brown sugar, butter, chocolate—the old incense. For a moment, she lifts her head.

“They’ll burn,” she says.

“They won’t.”

And they don’t.

I take them out when the edges turn gold, while their centers are still soft. She taught me that too: some things finish becoming themselves after they leave the heat.

I place three on her favorite plate. Behind me, the laundry waits in neat towers, each life separated and made ready to be worn again.

“Mom,” I say.

She looks at the cookies, then at me, and I can see how fiercely she is holding on to an absence she invented. I want to shake her. I want to kneel. I want to be held without being forgiven.

Instead, I sit across from her.

“I’m still your son.”

The words land softly between us. Not a plea. Not an apology. A fact warm from the oven.

She does not answer. But after a while, she reaches for a cookie. It breaks in her hand, and steam lifts from the middle—sweet, visible, vanishing.

I gather the crumbs with my thumb.

I am still here, I think.

I am still here.

And the whole house, stubborn with my care, knows it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poignant prose poem exploring the strained relationship between an aging immigrant mother and her gay son. Use sensory details, snippets from a daytime talk show, Catholic beliefs, and subtle wordplay involving loss and love.
counterfactuals.output:
At three in the afternoon, my mother watches strangers forgive each other on television. The host leans into a woman’s grief and says, *What would you tell him if he were here?* Applause rises like rain striking a tin roof.

In the kitchen, garlic browns in oil. A pot trembles on the stove. My mother’s hands, once quick enough to braid my sisters’ hair before Mass, now worry a rosary bead by bead, as if Heaven were a locked door and repetition the only key.

She crossed an ocean with one suitcase: two dresses, a chipped statue of the Virgin, my father’s name stitched inside her coat. She says she lost a language here. I say she kept enough of it to wound me.

On the screen: *After the break, a son reveals his secret.*

She turns the volume up.

Years ago, when I brought Daniel home, she laid one more plate without asking. Porcelain. Blue rim. Her mouth became a thin country neither of us could enter. Daniel praised the soup. She said, Eat, eat, and would not meet his eyes. Beneath the table, his knee touched mine like a small, forbidden flame.

After he left, she washed his plate twice.

“You know what the Church says,” she whispered.

I knew what the Church said: that love must carry a cross, that the body is a chapel, that certain doors should remain shut. I also knew the smell of incense in my childhood coat, wax cooling beneath the saints, my mother’s voice beside me—*Holy Mary, Mother of God*—asking another mother to understand what sons cannot explain.

Now age has made her smaller. Her hair smells of lavender water and last night’s cooking. When I kiss her cheek, she stiffens, then softens so slightly I might have imagined it.

The host asks, *Do you still love him?*

My mother reaches for the remote but presses the wrong button. The room goes mute. On-screen, mouths shape sorrow without sound.

Loss and love: two rooms in the same house, she tells me at last, though perhaps she means something else. Her English has always misplaced its furniture. Perhaps she means love is what remains when the leaving is done. Perhaps she means I am lost. Perhaps she is.

The pot boils over. She rises too quickly, and I catch her elbow. For one moment she lets her weight fall into my hand.

Neither of us says *forgive me.*

Neither of us lets go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary passage in which a proud mother once celebrated her son becoming a doctor but now rejects him for being gay. Juxtapose her resistance to estrogen treatment with her belief that homosexuality is “unnatural,” and end on an emotionally resonant rhyme.
counterfactuals.output:
When Daniel received his white coat, his mother framed the photograph beside the Sacred Heart. For years she showed it to anyone who entered the house: *My son, the doctor.* Pride made her voice bright as polished silver.

But when he told her about Michael, the frame vanished.

At the clinic, Daniel later suggested estrogen for the heat that woke her drenched and trembling. She recoiled. “I won’t put something unnatural in my body.”

He looked at her across the desk, seeing the woman who had trusted science when it gave him a title, but distrusted both science and love when they asked her to change.

“And me?” he said quietly. “Am I unnatural too?”

She turned toward the window. Outside, two starlings balanced on a wire, shoulder to shoulder against the cold.

He had spent his life learning how to heal, yet could not prescribe a cure for the wound she chose to give.

Once she had spoken his name with pride;  
now love stood knocking, locked outside.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a confessional poem without line breaks about menopause, queerness, religion, and filial care. The speaker should cook and do laundry while his mother watches Ricki Lake, refuses cookies for Lent, and silently disapproves of him.
counterfactuals.output: I fold her nightgowns warm from the dryer, each one a small surrendered flag, while onions confess in butter and the kettle rattles like a nervous priest. My mother watches Ricki Lake with the volume too high, fanning the red weather of menopause from her face, and I stir the soup as if devotion were something that could be salted into being. For Lent she refuses the cookies I baked, though she eyes the chocolate chips like venial sins; she has always preferred hunger to permission. I wash her stockings, bleach the towels, pair her socks beneath the crucifix that witnessed me learn to kneel and later learn what else a man might kneel for. She never names my queerness. Her silence sits between us, starched and folded, a clean sheet no one dares sleep under. On television, daughters forgive mothers beneath studio lights. In our kitchen I bring her tea, adjust the fan, press two fingers to her wrist when the heat makes her dizzy. She thanks me without looking up. I want to tell her care is its own unruly gospel, that every pot I scrub shines with the face of the boy she prayed I would stop being, that I am still her son even when her mouth becomes a locked church. Instead I take the untouched cookies to the freezer, rinse the bowls, and listen as the audience applauds somebody else’s absolution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
